theme: Make a joyful noise, all the earth as God’s people
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 100. It is one of the shortest and most familiar psalms. Read it slowly, as a closing song for the week, and notice the commands and the reasons.
settingTheScene: Psalm 100 is titled “A Psalm for giving thanks.” It was probably sung when worshipers entered the temple courts with their thank offerings, like the thanksgiving offerings of Leviticus 7. It is brief, with only five verses. It has been sung by Christians for centuries, often as a call to worship at the start of a service. It ends the series of “the LORD reigns” psalms with an invitation for the whole earth to join in.
observation: “Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth!” (v. 1).
“Serve the LORD with gladness! Come into his presence with singing!” (v. 2).
“Know that the LORD, he is God! It is he who made us, and we are his; we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture” (v. 3).
“Enter his gates with thanksgiving, and his courts with praise! Give thanks to him; bless his name!” (v. 4).
“For the LORD is good; his steadfast love endures forever, and his faithfulness to all generations” (v. 5).
There are seven commands: make a joyful noise, serve, come, know, enter, give thanks, bless.
There are three reasons: he is God and our maker, he is our shepherd, and he is good, loving, and faithful.
The psalm begins with “all the earth” and ends with “all generations.”
interpretation:
The psalm is a lesson in worship. It tells us what to do, and why. The commands are about joy, gladness, singing, thanksgiving, and praise. Worship is not meant to be a grim duty. It is meant to be glad service. The word “serve” in verse 2 is the same word used for the Levites’ work. All of life can be service, and the right attitude for it is gladness.

The reasons come in verse 3 and verse 5. First, “Know that the LORD, he is God.” Everything starts with who he is. Then, “It is he who made us, and we are his.” We did not make ourselves, and we do not belong to ourselves. This is a freeing thought. It means that we are not responsible for creating our own meaning. We were made, and we are his.

The image of sheep is especially fitting after reading Numbers. Israel were a flock, led by the cloud and the shepherd’s staff of Moses. Like sheep, they wandered, complained, and got into trouble. But they had a shepherd, and the psalm reminds us that we do, too. The one who leads is good.

The last verse gives three words that sum up God’s character: good, loving, and faithful. “His steadfast love endures forever” is the refrain of the whole Old Testament. It is the word used in Exodus 34:6, the name of God in the wilderness. The people failed again and again, but his love did not.

And the psalm is for everyone: “all the earth.” The church has always taken this seriously. The God of Israel is the God of the nations, and all are invited into his gates.
connection: Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11), and “I will build my church” (Matthew 16:18). Peter says that believers “were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” (1 Peter 2:25). Paul says that all things were created through Christ and for him (Colossians 1:16). Revelation 7:9-10 shows people from every nation joining the worship around the throne.
application:
Say this psalm aloud as a prayer of thanks. Name three specific things for which you are thankful.

Remember that you were made by God and belong to him. Let that settle your restlessness.

Invite someone to church or to a conversation about Christ this week.
prayerPrompts: Enter God’s gates with thanksgiving, naming specific things you are thankful for.
Thank him that you are the sheep of his pasture.
Praise him that his faithfulness reaches to every generation.
